The idea to keep in mind

A sensation is information, not a verdict.

A tight chest, restless hands, or a heavy feeling can be worth noticing. No sensation, on its own, tells a therapist what happened in your past or what diagnosis you have.

Understanding the approach

Body awareness can join the conversation.

Somatic-informed therapy is an umbrella description, not one standardized treatment. A clinician may bring attention to sensations, posture, movement, or the surrounding environment alongside thoughts, feelings, relationships, and behavior. Different body-oriented approaches have different theories and training requirements.

Somatic Experiencing is one specific model within this wider landscape. Its developer describes attending to bodily experience while pacing work with stress and trauma. That description is the model's perspective; it is not proof that every bodily response reflects trapped trauma or that a particular exercise releases it. An informed style does not establish a Somatic Experiencing Practitioner credential.

The practical value of paying attention to the body must be considered in your actual circumstances. Some people find internal attention useful; others feel more alarmed, disconnected, or uncomfortable. A responsive therapist can explain a suggestion, offer alternatives, and stop when it is not helpful. Medical symptoms also deserve medical judgment rather than automatically being interpreted as emotional.

Sources somatic psychotherapy mindfulness

In plain language

You remain in charge of participation.

You can keep your eyes open, decline an exercise, choose an external point of attention, or return to talking. Consent is an ongoing part of the work, not a box checked at the beginning.

A worked example

The meeting ends. Your shoulders are still braced.

An ordinary fictional example of noticing a response without assigning it a hidden meaning.

Fictional teaching example. Not a diagnosis, a client story, or an assigned exercise.

01

What is noticed

After a tense meeting, Alex realizes their shoulders are raised and their hands are gripping a notebook. They had been focused on whether they answered well.

02

What is not assumed

The clinician does not decide that a particular posture proves a childhood event. They ask how Alex understands the meeting and whether noticing the sensations feels manageable.

03

What might be explored

With permission, the conversation could include the room, the support of the chair, and what changes when attention moves away from replaying the exchange. Alex can choose to stay with verbal discussion instead.

Why does pacing matter here?

A small, tolerable observation is different from pushing someone into an intense bodily experience. Alex might notice a change, no change, or increased discomfort. Each response is information for adapting the work, not evidence that they are doing therapy wrong.

The point is not to achieve a particular feeling on command. A useful next step might still involve clarifying feedback at work, considering a relationship pattern, or getting medical advice about persistent physical symptoms. A body-focused exercise does not replace those tasks.

Sources somatic psychotherapy mindfulness

Fit, choice and limitations

Do not confuse a broad influence with a proven explanation.

No hidden-history detector

Body sensations, movements, or emotional reactions do not independently verify memories, explain a disease, or prove a specific trauma. A clinician should not present an interpretation as a recovered fact.

Evidence and scope vary

Research on one defined protocol does not automatically support every practice called somatic. Ask which approach the clinician means, what their relevant training is, and how it fits with other appropriate care.

Sources somatic psychotherapy mindfulness

Go a little deeper

Four distinctions behind the label.

These are descriptions of possible elements, not instructions for trauma processing on your own.

01Internal and external attentionAttention does not have to stay inside the body.Read more +

Internal attention might include noticing warmth, tension, or movement. External attention might include the room, a sound, or a stable visual point. A clinician can discuss which feels more workable rather than treating inward focus as inherently better.

If attention increases panic or disconnection, that is a reason to pause and adapt, not to push harder.

02PacingIntensity is not the measure of good work.Read more +

A therapist may move between difficult material and what feels more manageable. The reason should be explained in ordinary language. You do not need an overwhelming emotional release to make an appointment worthwhile.

A small shift in awareness may be enough to consider before returning to the rest of your life and goals.

03Movement and choiceAny suggested activity needs consent and a purpose.Read more +

A clinician might discuss an ordinary change of posture or another gentle activity. Not every somatic-informed session includes movement, and no activity is automatically suitable for every body. Accessibility, pain, culture, and personal preference matter.

This page does not authorize touch or imply it is part of M.F.T. services. Ask about the actual clinician's boundaries and methods.

04IntegrationWhat you notice should connect to the wider work.Read more +

Noticing a response can lead back to a question about a situation, belief, relationship, or practical need. Sensations are not a substitute for understanding context.

The approach should support your goals rather than turn therapy into constant monitoring of the body.

Sources somatic psychotherapy mindfulness

Inside the work

A collaborative sequence, not a required exercise.

01

Clarify the goal

Discuss why you are considering care and whether body-oriented attention might serve the work. Tell the clinician about relevant medical or accessibility concerns.

02

Explain and agree

A suggestion should come with a plain-language purpose and a genuine option to decline. Ask what alternatives are available.

03

Notice in manageable amounts

The clinician and client can check whether the experience is tolerable and useful, and change direction when it is not.

04

Connect and review

Consider what the observation adds to understanding daily life. Revisit whether this element belongs in the ongoing plan.

Your questions, answered

More to know before choosing.

Is this the same as massage or bodywork?

No. This page concerns a way of integrating attention to bodily experience into psychotherapy. It does not describe massage, manipulation, or touch services at M.F.T. The therapist should explain the specific boundaries of the service offered.

Do I have to close my eyes?

No. An exercise should be optional and adapted. Eyes-open attention, external orientation, ordinary conversation, or another approach may be preferable.

What if focusing on my body makes me anxious?

Tell the clinician and pause. More intensity is not automatically more therapeutic. The response may call for different pacing, a different focus, or another method.

Can physical symptoms be caused by something medical?

Yes. A therapy explanation should not replace appropriate medical assessment. New or concerning symptoms need the relevant level of medical care, not an assumption that they are only stress.

Does somatic-informed mean certified in Somatic Experiencing?

No. A broad description of influence is different from completing training or certification in a named model. The clinician connections here are limited to the recorded profile wording.

For practical questions, contact the support team. Please keep clinical details out of the initial email.
